By recapitulating complex tissue microenvironments, multi-organ interactions, and patient-specific biology, these systems are bridging long-standing gaps in the drug development and clinical application pipelines. Here, we synthesize advances in organoids, OOCs, and other bioengineered technologies for translational medicine to identify remaining gaps, including challenges in reproducibility, validation, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging opportunities at the intersection of synthetic biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and genetic engineering are positioning NAMs not merely as improved experimental tools but as foundational platforms for accelerating therapeutic discovery and enabling personalized medicine at scale.

title: EPCR expression marks CD150neg deeply dormant long-term hematopoietic stem cells
abstract: Cell surface expression of the Slam family member CD150 is widely used for the prospective isolation of multipotent long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs). Here, we identify a bona fide endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) + CD150 − HSC subset, termed LT-HSC2, that sustains serial multi-lineage reconstitution. Long-term label-retaining assays reveal that LT-HSC2s are more deeply dormant than conventional EPCR + CD150 + LT-HSC1s, exhibit reduced cell cycle activation in response to inflammatory stress, and preserve stemness for prolonged periods in vivo . Moreover, combining EPCR with established HSC and multipotent progenitor (MPP) markers resolves the earliest stages of lineage divergence toward megakaryocytic/erythroid-biased CD150 + and lymphoid-biased CD150 − trajectories. Thus, EPCR expression in HSCs and MPPs is associated with increased stemness, whereas CD150 expression does not encompass the full spectrum of long-term repopulating HSCs. Our findings establish EPCR + CD150 − LT-HSC2s as a distinct, exceptionally dormant stem-cell subset and reveal an additional layer of HSC heterogeneity governing self-renewal, decreased stress sensitvity. and earliest lineage priming.

title: Electroconductive patch promotes heart repair by directing epicardial cells toward endothelial fate
abstract: Whether epicardium-derived cells (EPDCs) can differentiate into endothelial cells after myocardial infarction (MI) remains unclear. Considering the heart's electrical dependence, we asked if restoring electrical conduction could direct this potential. Using cardiac patches with tunable electroconductivity and genetic fate-mapping approaches in mice, we found that patches matching native myocardial electroconductivity (10 -4 -10 -3 S/cm) specifically promoted proliferation and endothelial differentiation of WT1 + EPDCs, rescuing cardiac function. Single-cell transcriptomic sequencing revealed that electroconductive patches drove WT1 + EPDCs into a distinct WT1 + TRPC3 + CD93 + transitional state. These cells differentiated into endothelial cells via TRPC3-Ca 2+ signaling and integrated into functional vessels. Inhibiting TRPC3 blocked differentiation and reduced infarct vascularization. Thus, improving electrical conduction unlocks and directs the endothelial differentiation of WT1 + EPDCs, offering a strategy for post-MI repair.

title: Niche-reprogramming CAR T therapy improves skeletal muscle regeneration and function in preclinical murine models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a fatal neuromuscular disorder with no cure. Emerging dystrophin-restoring gene therapies target mutant myofibers but face challenges in efficacy and toxicities, underscoring the need for new treatments. Current therapies do not address chronic inflammation and muscle fibrosis, key pathologies creating a pathological muscle microenvironment that impairs dystrophic muscle function and regeneration. Here, we identify urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR) as a shared surface marker on subsets of macrophages and fibro-adipogenic progenitors exhibiting strong pro-inflammatory and fibrogenic signatures in DMD. Notably, uPAR-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells selectively eliminate these pathogenic subpopulations, remodel the muscle microenvironment, and enhance dystrophic muscle regeneration and force production; they also improve diaphragm and respiratory function, addressing an unmet clinical need and a major cause of DMD mortality. These findings establish uPAR CAR T cells as a niche-remodeling regenerative immunotherapy that simultaneously addresses multiple DMD pathologies and improves dystrophic muscle regeneration and function.
